narrative:
Your application was denied because the admissions model assessed a 73.8 percent probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high risk, and the university concluded that admitting you would likely lead to an unsuccessful outcome. Three factors drove this decision more than anything else.

The strongest influence was your class standing in your third year of study. You are currently in the first decile, meaning you are at the very bottom of your class based on your Year 3 grades. Among admitted students, the average class standing is around the sixth decile, so your academic performance in a critical year placed you well behind the typical successful applicant. This was the largest push toward a failure prediction.

Your LSAT score also weighed heavily. At 26, it is far below the average score of 37 among students who were accepted into similar programs. A lower LSAT score is strongly associated with difficulty passing the bar, so this reinforced the risk.

Your undergraduate GPA, however, told a slightly different story. At 2.90, it is below the average of 3.23, but this factor actually nudged the prediction toward passing, meaning it had a small protective influence. Unfortunately, it was not enough to overcome the negative signals from your third-year standing and LSAT score.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic record in your final year, especially by moving out of the lowest decile. Consider retaking the LSAT after dedicated preparation to boost your score. You might also strengthen your application with additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program that demonstrates your ability to handle rigorous legal study. These steps would directly address the factors that led to this denial.
